anomaly_def.Name: SQL Workload Logic Anomaly + Schema and Index Design Anomaly + Query Plan Selection Anomaly
anomaly_def.Description:
SQL Workload Logic Anomaly: Application-level SQL or transaction design forces the engine to touch more data, rows, or time than business logic truly demands.
Schema and Index Design Anomaly: Physical table, index, partition, or datatype choices do not fit the workload’s access patterns, forcing otherwise well-written statements into inefficient access paths.
Query Plan Selection Anomaly: The optimizer chooses a substantially sub-optimal execution plan despite having reasonably accurate statistics, due to cost-model or plan-reuse issues.

When these three root causes coexist, symptoms at every observation layer intensify and blur together: statements originally written with broad predicates or poor batching trigger full-table or non-covering index scans because the necessary supporting indexes or partitions are missing, while the optimizer simultaneously misjudges the remaining access options, producing erratic plan flips between inefficient scans and explosive nested loops. As a result, the same queries may alternate between long tail latencies and catastrophic stalls, saturating I/O and memory, prolonging lock holds, and cascading into application timeouts, deadlocks, and retry storms. Execution-statistics and performance dashboards show extreme variance: high logical I/O, frequent plan cache churn, bloated temp usage, and atypical CPU spikes during both read- and write-heavy windows.

Causally, sub-optimal SQL logic (e.g., non-sargable predicates, Cartesian joins, oversized batches) magnifies the penalty of a weak physical design by driving large row counts through tables that lack selective or covering indexes. In turn, the impoverished index/partition layout restricts the optimizer’s viable plan space, increasing its reliance on brittle cost estimates; even small cardinality errors or bind-value changes cause dramatic plan swings. Meanwhile, mischosen plans reinforce the workload’s inefficiencies, amplifying I/O and contention, which lengthen transaction lifetimes imposed by the original poor logic. The feedback loop among ill-formed SQL, mismatched schema structures, and unstable plan selection escalates resource consumption and variability, degrading both transactional and analytical operations across the system.

entry.official_definition: Write timeout for X Plugin network communication.
entry.trigger_condition: A MySQL X Protocol write operation exceeds mysqlx_write_timeout.
entry.workload_impact: The X Protocol network write operation times out.
entry.default_behavior: Defined as a MySQL X Plugin system variable.
entry.cause_analysis: This timeout is usually triggered when network data is not acknowledged, received, or written within the configured transport-level waiting window.
entry.solution_guidance: Inspect packet loss, transport latency, client responsiveness, proxy behavior, and whether slow consumers or unstable links are delaying network progress.
